source.title: Expand Neurons, Not Parameters
source.authors: Linghao Kong; Inimai Subramanian; Yonadav G. Shavit; Micah Adler; Dan Alistarh; N. Shavit

record.file_problem: Minor PDF text-extraction artifacts, but the paper is readable and appears complete.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether an architectural change—expanding neuron count at a fixed non-zero parameter budget—reduces feature interference, using feature-capacity and cosine-similarity measures rather than auditing the share of neurons with named jobs.
record.gate_note: The results bear on V4’s architectural/interference mechanism, but do not directly measure the fraction of interpretable neurons. The paper does not test the Qwen3-32B audit, scale to language models or trillions of parameters, evaluate the InceptionV1 example, build attribution graphs, or test explanation quality on held-out activating examples. Accuracy results and cited findings are not included as rows because they do not themselves measure neuron interpretability or interference.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version of the claim. It trains tiny Boolean-DNF and vision MLPs that are deliberately given more features than neurons. It then measures superposition proxies (summed feature capacity, mean weight cosine similarity) after splitting neurons at a fixed non-zero parameter budget. It never measures the share of neurons with one interpretable job, and it does not evaluate tools, regularization or modern architectures in trained models. V4 concerns that share, so these geometric proxies are a related but different construct and are recorded under fits_no_version. The authors also frame their results as confirming capacity-driven superposition, the reverse framing of the essay's thesis. Still, a toy setup engineered for superposition pressure cannot show whether real networks' neurons are clean.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that redistributing a fixed non-zero parameter budget across more neurons reduces feature interference and improves accuracy, especially in high-superposition regimes. They state that random splits recover much of the gain and that disjoint weight allocation, not width alone, is key. They frame this as support for the superposition hypothesis and call it a small-scale proof of concept. Transformer-scale tests are left to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses Fixed Parameter Expansion: it splits weights across more neurons at a fixed non-zero parameter budget, then measures feature-capacity and geometric interference proxies. It does not label neuron jobs or test explanations on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that effects vary with neuron count and feature demand; gains are strongest in constrained settings. It compares clause-aware and random splitting, and reports cosine-similarity results across literal counts. It also describes expansion-factor, timing, depth, and dataset variations.

fits_no_version.finding: In 8-neuron Boolean DNF classifiers, splitting neurons at fixed non-zero parameter count raised summed feature capacity in every literal setting. For example, at 128 literals it rose from 7.70 to 16.87 (clause-split) and 13.80 (random-split). Mean weight cosine similarity fell in every setting (e.g. 0.262 to about 0.105). Gains were largest under high feature-to-neuron pressure. Clause-split models also showed lower edge-collision rates and higher clause-recovery ARI (Fig. A7, not tabulated).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small networks forced into superposition, allocating a fixed parameter budget across more neurons reduces feature interference (higher feature capacity, more orthogonal neurons) and improves accuracy.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306 (2026)
record.problems: The evidence is mainly from controlled Boolean tasks and vision classifiers, not language-model neuron audits. Feature capacity and cosine similarity are proxies for interference, not direct measurements of a neuron’s job or of the share of neurons that are interpretable. The paper itself describes the mechanistic analyses as preliminary and its settings as relatively small-scale.
record.rows_left_out: Accuracy outcomes, circuit/cluster descriptions without separately reported numerical values, and cited results were left out because they do not directly measure the interpretability/interference outcomes represented in V4 or are not reported as numerical or explicit per-condition results in the included tables.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron audit or job shares.
No language models, MoE models or scale beyond small MLPs/CNN heads.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron reanalysis.
No measure of the share of interpretable neurons; no comparison of tools, regularization or modern architectures in trained networks; no InceptionV1-sized estimates.
No attribution graphs or replacement-model comparison.
No test of explanations against held-out firing.

record.verdict_notes: The reader labelled V4 as supported, but the rows only show interference proxies in toy models built to have more features than neurons. The authors explicitly attribute polysemanticity to feature-to-neuron capacity pressure. That attribution is, if anything, contrary in spirit to the essay's 'not capacity' thesis, but it does not bear on how often real models' neurons are interpretable. The mechanistic analyses are described by the authors as preliminary. Accuracy results were rightly left out of the rows.

versions.untested_parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or estimates of one-job, two-job, or not-understood shares.
No audit across language models, dense and mixture-of-experts models, or models up to trillions of parameters.
No analysis of InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, or recursive generalization.

Tests width expansion and feature-interference proxies in controlled Boolean tasks and some vision settings, but not the share of neurons interpretable under improved tools, the essay’s InceptionV1-sized estimates, or the separate effects of architecture, regularization, and tools.
No attribution-graph evaluation or comparison to a trained replacement model.
No test of explanations against where neurons fire on held-out examples.
No automated simulation scoring of neuron explanations on new text.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Boolean DNF classifiers with 8 original neurons, across the reported literal counts and both splitting methods
reader_labels.reason: Feature capacity rises and mean neuron cosine similarity falls relative to dense baselines in the reported settings, consistent with reduced interference after width expansion; rows FC-12 through FR-128 and CC-12 through CR-128. These are proxies, not estimates of the share of interpretable neurons.
